title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Context (from the neighbouring pages): Euler is reducing a variational problem for a curve to quadratures. The curve lies in the plane z = my + nx through the origin. Its distance from the origin is v, with vv = xx + yy + (my+nx)^2. The variables are u = y/x and p = dy/dx, and ss = 1 + pp + (mp+n)^2 = (ds/dx)^2. The weight function w(v) enters only through r = w/(w'v). The Euler–Lagrange equation has been brought to the form dΦ + r dψ = 0, where dΦ = γ du/(1+uu+(mu+n)^2) and dψ = γ dp/(1+pp+(mp+n)^2).

On this page Euler finishes the coefficient matching that makes these arctangent differentials. Setting tan Φ = αu + β, identity in u gives αγ = mm+1, βγ = mn and γ(ββ+1) = α(nn+1). Eliminating α and β gives γ² = (mm+1)(nn+1) − m²n² = mm+nn+1. Hence γ = √(mm+nn+1), α = (mm+1)/γ and β = mn/γ.

Homogenising with u = y/x gives the quadratic-form identity xx + yy + (my+nx)^2 = (γ/α)(xx + (αy+βx)^2). In modern terms this diagonalises the induced metric Q(x,y) = dx² + dy² + (m dy + n dx)² of the plane z = my + nx, written in its projected coordinates (x, y). The pair (x, αy+βx), scaled by √(γ/α), is an orthonormal frame in that plane.

With δ² = α/γ = (mm+1)/(mm+nn+1), Euler gets x = δv cos Φ and αy + βx = δv sin Φ. So (v, Φ) are exactly Euclidean polar coordinates in the plane containing the curve. Once Φ is known as a function of v, x and y follow, and the problem is solved.

In §37 the same substitution is applied to the slope: tan ψ = αp + β, with 1 + (αp+β)^2 = (α/γ) ss. Then ψ is the polar direction angle of the tangent in the same frame. The main equation becomes dψ + (w'v/w) dΦ = 0.

On the next page Euler shows ψ = Φ + arctan(v dΦ/dv). This is the standard planar central-symmetric problem, leading to a Clairaut/Snell-type first integral of the form v·w(v)·sin(angle between tangent and radius) = const. In essence the page recognises that a plane through the centre reduces the 3-D problem to a 2-D one, via an oblique-to-orthonormal coordinate change.
errors: The print has 'nu' instead of 'nn' in the denominator of β: it should read β = mn/√(mm+nn+1). This is a typographical error in the original.
In §37 the closing parenthesis is missing in (α/γ)(1+pp+(mp+n)^2; it should read (α/γ)(1+pp+(mp+n)^2) = (α/γ)ss. Typographical only.
No mathematical errors: γ² = mm+nn+1, the factorisation of the quadratic form, and the polar representation all check.

ideas.what: Integrating dΦ = γ du/(1+uu+(mu+n)^2) as an arctangent by completing the square, with tan Φ = αu + β
ideas.modern_name: Completing the square / standard arctangent integral

ideas.what: Diagonalising the induced metric of the plane z = my + nx to get orthonormal (polar) coordinates (v, Φ) in that plane
ideas.modern_name: Gram–Schmidt / reduction of a positive quadratic form to a sum of squares; polar coordinates in an inclined plane
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (reduction of quadratic forms, 1759) and Gauss; standard
ideas.where_published: Similar coordinate changes occur in Euler's analytic geometry of surfaces (Introductio, vol. 2, appendix); exact parallel unsure

ideas.what: Representing the tangent direction by tan ψ = αp + β in the same frame, so that ψ − Φ is the angle between tangent and radius vector
ideas.modern_name: Angle between radius vector and tangent in polar coordinates (precursor to a Clairaut-type first integral)
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (E65), central-force and isoperimetric examples

deep.surprise_reason: The page performs routine algebra: completing the square and an orthonormal change of frame in a plane through the origin. It reduces an apparently spatial variational problem to the classical planar central one. Everything is correct and standard, with nothing absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: 'β = mn/√(mm+nu+1)' should be 'β = mn/√(mm+nn+1)'. The print itself shows 'n u', which is a misprint for 'nn'.
§37: '1+(αp+β)^2 = (α/γ)(1+pp+(mp+n)^2 = (α/γ)ss' is missing a closing parenthesis after (mp+n)^2. This is also in the print.
The angle symbol is printed as Φ (phi) throughout. The transcription alternates between Φ and φ; they denote the same angle.
